title: Parameter tuples characterize germs of flat quasi-finite affine-space charts
statement:
Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-algebraic-closure], $X$ a finite-type $k$-scheme [def-pc-scheme; def-weil-finite-type-morphism], and $x\in X$ a closed point [def-weil-closed-points]. Write $R=\mathcal O_{X,x}$ for its local ring [def-weil-pbc-module-stalk], $\mathfrak m$ for its maximal ideal, and identify $\kappa(x)=R/\mathfrak m$ with $k$ via the structure map [def-weil-residue-field]. The ring $R$ is Noetherian [def-weil-pbc-noetherian-ring]. Assume $R$ is Cohen–Macaulay, meaning $\operatorname{depth}(R)=\dim R$ [def-weil-pbc-depth; def-weil-pbc-krull-dimension-ring]. Let $d\ge0$, let $V\subseteq X$ be an open neighbourhood of $x$, and let $f_1,\ldots,f_d\in\Gamma(V,\mathcal O_X)$. Define $f:V\to\mathbf A^d_k$ by these coordinates [def-sbc-affine-space], put $a_i=f_i(x)\in k$, and let $t_i=(f_i)_x-a_i\in\mathfrak m$. The following are equivalent:

(i) There is an open neighbourhood $x\in U\subseteq V$ such that $f|_U:U\to\mathbf A^d_k$ is quasi-finite and flat [pqf-def-quasifinite; def-weil-flat-morphism].

(ii) $\dim R=d$ and $\sqrt{(t_1,\ldots,t_d)R}=\mathfrak m$.

A tuple of $d$ elements in the maximal ideal of a $d$-dimensional Noetherian local ring whose generated ideal has radical the maximal ideal is called a system of parameters. Equivalently, its quotient ring is nonzero of Krull dimension zero. The neighbourhood in (i) may be chosen affine. In particular the criterion concerns any prescribed representatives $f_i$, without altering their germs or their coordinate values.

source.place: XVIII Lemma 2.6, p. 552, first proof paragraph (germs of flat quasi-finite maps are systems of parameters). Algebraic ingredients: Stacks Tag 00R4 (algebra.tex, lemma-CM-over-regular-flat), Tag 01TH (morphisms.tex, lemma-quasi-finite-at-point-characterize), Tag 01TI (morphisms.tex, lemma-quasi-finite-points-open), and Tag 00RC (algebra.tex, theorem-openness-flatness).

proof.text: Work on an affine neighbourhood of $x$ contained in $V$ without changing any coordinate section except by restriction. Explicitly, the finite-type hypothesis supplies an affine neighbourhood $W_0=\operatorname{Spec}B_0$ with $B_0$ a finitely generated $k$-algebra. The basic-open basis gives $h\in B_0$ with $x\in D(h)\subseteq W_0\cap V$. The principal-open assertion gives an affine scheme $W=D(h)=\operatorname{Spec}B$, $B=(B_0)_h$. If $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ generate $B_0$ over $k$, their images together with $h^{-1}$ generate $B$; hence $B$ is finite type over $k$. Write $\mathfrak q$ for the maximal ideal of $B$ corresponding to the closed point $x$, and $b_i=f_i|_W$ (the index $i$ now ranges from $1$ to $d$). The affine-stalk theorem identifies $R=B_{\mathfrak q}$ compatibly with these germs. Put $P=k[T_1,\ldots,T_d]$ and $\varphi:P\to B$, $T_i\mapsto b_i$. The $k$-algebra generators of $B$ also generate it over $P$, so $\varphi$ is finite type. Apply the pointwise affine-pair criterion, using the same pair $W,\operatorname{Spec}P$ around every point of $W$, to conclude that $f|_W$ is locally of finite type. Finally $B$ is Noetherian by the finite-type-over-a-field theorem.

source.place: Tags 00E0 (lemma-Zariski-topology), 00E4 (lemma-standard-open), 00FN (lemma-Noetherian-permanence); Schemes 01I3, 01HS, 01HV; Morphisms 01T2. Explicit generator argument for restrictions.

proof.text: The inverse image of $\mathfrak q$ in $P$ is $\mathfrak n=(T_1-a_1,\ldots,T_d-a_d)$: reduction modulo $\mathfrak q$ is evaluation at $a=(a_i)$ in $k$. Indeed $Q(T)-Q(a)$ is in that ideal, by changing one variable at a time and using $T_i^r-a_i^r=(T_i-a_i)\sum_{j=0}^{r-1}T_i^{r-1-j}a_i^j$. Thus $P/\mathfrak n=k$ and $\mathfrak n$ is maximal. Set $A=P_{\mathfrak n}$. Polynomial regularity makes $P$ Noetherian and $A$ a Noetherian regular local ring, and the maximal-localization dimension theorem gives $\dim A=d$. The affine-stalk identification makes the prescribed map at $x$ precisely the local map $\psi:A\to R=B_{\mathfrak q}$, $T_i-a_i\mapsto t_i$. Its closed-fibre ideal is $\mathfrak nR=I=(t_1,\ldots,t_d)R\subseteq\mathfrak m$.

Let $J=(b_1-a_1,\ldots,b_d-a_d)B$. The affine fibre over $a$ has ring $F=B\otimes_P k\cong B/J$. To see the latter identification explicitly, $b\otimes c\mapsto cb\bmod J$ is balanced because $T_i$ acts on $k$ as $a_i$; its inverse sends $b\bmod J$ to $b\otimes1$. The point over $x$ corresponds to $\overline{\mathfrak q}=\mathfrak q/J$, a maximal ideal with residue field $k$. Localizing the quotient gives $C=F_{\overline{\mathfrak q}}\cong B_{\mathfrak q}/JB_{\mathfrak q}=R/I$. In particular $C$ is nonzero, since $I\subseteq\mathfrak m$ and $R/I$ surjects onto $R/\mathfrak m=k$. Notice that $F$ is finite type over $k$, since the images of generators of $B$ generate $B/J$.

source.place: Tag 00CT (proposition-localize-quotient); Schemes Tag 01JQ affine fibre product formula (lemma-fibre-product-affines), and explicit balanced maps for the evaluation quotient.

proof.text: For this proper ideal $I$ of the local ring $R$, one has $\sqrt I=\mathfrak m$ if and only if $\dim(R/I)=0$. Primes of $R/I$ correspond, by inverse image and quotient, to primes of $R$ containing $I$: primality in either direction follows from the equation $uv\bmod I=(u\bmod I)(v\bmod I)$. Every such prime lies in $\mathfrak m$. If $\sqrt I=\mathfrak m$, each such prime contains $\mathfrak m$, so it is $\mathfrak m$, and $R/I$ has one prime and dimension zero. Conversely dimension zero precludes a strict chain from a prime over $I$ to $\mathfrak m$, so the latter is the only prime over $I$. The radical-intersection formula then gives $\sqrt I=\mathfrak m$. This also proves the quotient-ring reformulation in the statement, under its stipulated equality $\dim R=d$.

The ring quasi-finiteness/zero-fibre-dimension equivalence applies to the finite-type map $P\to B$ at $\mathfrak q$. Its fibre is the finite-type $k$-algebra $F$ of step 3 and its indicated prime $\overline{\mathfrak q}$ is maximal. Therefore the closed-point dimension theorem identifies $\dim_{\overline{\mathfrak q}}\operatorname{Spec}F$ with $\dim F_{\overline{\mathfrak q}}=\dim C$. The equivalence says exactly that $P\to B$ is quasi-finite at $\mathfrak q$ if and only if $\dim C=0$. By the affine-pair definition of scheme quasi-finiteness, and its independence of the affine pair furnished by the isolated-fibre/affine-pairs theorem, this is equivalent to $f|_W$ being quasi-finite at $x$. For the converse use of that theorem, a morphism quasi-finite at $x$ has $x$ isolated in its fibre, so the theorem applies to the particular affine pair $W,\mathbf A^d_k$. Thus this equivalence works for the prescribed $W$ and the prescribed representatives.

Assume (i). Intersect its neighbourhood with $W$; the local ring and local map at $x$ do not change, and the open singleton in the fibre of this intersection is open in the fibre of $W$, since the intersection is open in $W$. Step 5 gives $\dim C=0$, hence step 4 gives $\sqrt I=\mathfrak m$. Flatness at $x$ says that $\psi:A\to R$ is flat. Both local rings are Noetherian, so apply the flat height/dimension formula to $A\to R$ at their maximal ideals. Localizing a local ring at its maximal ideal changes nothing, and the formula is $\dim R=\dim A+\dim(R/\mathfrak nR)=d+0=d$. This proves both assertions in (ii).

Assume (ii). By steps 3 and 4 the closed fibre of $\psi:A\to R$ is nonzero of dimension zero, and by step 2 $\dim A=d$. Consequently $\dim R=\dim A+\dim(R/\mathfrak nR)$. The source $A$ is regular Noetherian local; the target $R$ is Noetherian local and Cohen–Macaulay by hypothesis; and $\psi$ is local. These are exactly the three hypotheses of miracle flatness, which gives flatness of $A\to R$. The quasi-finiteness at $x$ also follows from step 5.

source.place: Tag 00R4 (lemma-CM-over-regular-flat), applied to the local map already constructed.

proof.text: The flat-over-localization equivalence applied to $P\to A=P_{\mathfrak n}$ turns flatness of the $A$-module $R=B_{\mathfrak q}$ into flatness over $P$. Apply the Noetherian flat-locus neighbourhood theorem to $P\to B$, $M=B$ and $\mathfrak q$: $P$ is Noetherian by step 2, $B$ is a finite-type $P$-algebra by step 1, and $B$ is generated by $1$ as a $B$-module. Obtain $g\notin\mathfrak q$ such that $B_{\mathfrak q'}$ is flat over $P$ whenever $g\notin\mathfrak q'$. For each such $\mathfrak q'$ with $\mathfrak p'=\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak q')$, the same flat-over-localization equivalence identifies this with flatness over $P_{\mathfrak p'}$. The affine-stalk theorem and the definition of flatness therefore show that $f$ is flat at every point of $D(g)\subseteq W$.

The quasi-finite-points-open theorem applied to $f|_W$ supplies an open $Q\subseteq W$ containing $x$ on which the morphism is locally quasi-finite. Choose a basic open $D(v)$ of $W$ with $x\in D(v)\subseteq Q\cap D(g)$. The principal-open theorem makes $U=D(v)$ affine. Its local maps are unchanged from those of $W$, hence it is flat by step 8. For each $y\in U\subseteq Q$, the morphism $f|_W$ is quasi-finite at $y$ by the definition of $Q$, and it is locally of finite type by step 1. Apply the quasi-finite-at-point-isolated theorem to $f|_W$ at $y$: the singleton of $y$ is open in its $W$-fibre. Its intersection with $U$ is the same singleton and is open in the $U$-fibre. Thus every point of $U$ is isolated in its fibre. Finally $B_v$ is generated over $P$ by the finite generating set of $B$ together with $v^{-1}$, so the pointwise affine-pair criterion, with this same pair around every point, makes $U\to\operatorname{Spec}P$ locally of finite type. Also $B_v$ is finite type over $k$, so the finite-type affine Noetherian theorem gives the descending chain condition on closed subsets of $U$. Every open of $U$ is quasi-compact: if an open cover had no finite subcover, successively adding a member not already covered would give a strictly increasing infinite chain of open finite unions, contradicting that descending chain condition on complements. The inverse image of each affine target open is an open of $U$, hence quasi-compact. Thus the morphism is quasi-compact and locally of finite type, hence of finite type. By the definition, finite type together with isolated fibre points is quasi-finite. This proves (i) with $U$ affine. Every coordinate throughout is the restriction of the original $f_i$, so all original germs and coordinate values are preserved. If $d=0$, $P=A=k$, $I=0$, and the same argument uses the empty tuple; it says precisely that $R$ has dimension zero. No step assumes $d>0$, reducedness, or a separable chart.
